notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes on Job 23 below. The main commentaries I read were Enduring Word (Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, Gill, Wesley's Notes, Clarke, Matthew Henry, Precept Austin and the Bible Hub/StudyLight pages for vv. 10 and 17.

**Gaps.** I found nothing from Calvin or another Reformed writer, nothing Lutheran (1517.org, LCMS) and no Orthodox source. I found no page from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org; the NET Bible appears only as a translation quoted on Bible Hub. I couldn't open Haydock's Catholic commentary on this chapter, and I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those areas are left out.

**Where the traditions differ (detail under each verse):**
- **Bold or irreverent (vv. 3–7):** Spurgeon and Guzik praise Job's boldness. Wesley (Methodist) says Job was being irreverent. Matthew Henry calls the complaint "peevish."
- **Christ read into the text:** Gill (a Calvinist Baptist) applies vv. 3 and 10 to Christ and His righteousness counted to believers. The others mostly don't.
- **"Gold" (v. 10):** some say the trial purifies Job; others say it only proves he was pure all along.
- **The meaning of v. 17:** this depends on how the Hebrew is translated.

---

**v. 1** – Ellicott: Job answers Eliphaz's hints by longing for God and insisting he is innocent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/23-1.htm
– Gill: Job doesn't speak to Eliphaz directly. As proof of innocence, he asks only to bring his case before God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html

**v. 2** – Pulpit: whatever his friends say, Job still complains as bitterly as ever, and his suffering is even worse than his complaint. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Clarke: Job got neither conviction nor comfort from his friends' speeches. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-23.html
– Guzik: his friends' counsel only made his agony worse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/
– Gill: the "hand" could be Job's own, hanging weak, or God's hand pressing on him. Some render the first line as "my sighing is counted rebellion." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html
– Wesley: "today" means even now, despite their "pretended consolations." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html

**v. 3** – Guzik: Job felt cut off from God, a small but real echo of Christ's forsakenness on the cross. He quotes Spurgeon: the deepest desire of grieving saints is not escape but "to get at their God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/
– Pulpit: this is the cry of the desolate soul. Job pictures himself rising to God's throne, not God coming down to him. It took later revelation to show that God is near (Acts 17:28). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Gill (Baptist): "His seat" could be the mercy seat, reached through Christ, or the judgment seat, where a believer stands only in Christ's righteousness. Here Job mainly means a fair hearing of his case. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html
– Wesley: Job wants God's throne or judgment seat, but God hides His face. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html

**v. 4** – Pulpit: this reverses Job's earlier timidity in ch. 9 ("How should man be just with God?"). "Arguments" is courtroom language. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Guzik: Job wants to be cleared before his accusing friends, not just comforted. He quotes Mason, who says Job in effect wants to sue God for defamation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/
– Gill: Job is defending his cause against false charges, not seeking to be justified by his own works. Before God, a believer's arguments come from Christ's work and God's promises. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html

**v. 5** – Pulpit: this mood is "too bold for a creature" and wouldn't suit Christians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Wesley: if God showed Job a hidden sin, Job would humble himself and accept the punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html
– Gill: Job would finally learn why God was contending with him, and he would accept God's verdict, though not his friends'. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html

**v. 6** – Pulpit: better translated "He would give heed to me" than the KJV's "put strength in me." God wouldn't simply crush Job with force. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Wesley: God would use His power for Job, helping him plead his case. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html
– Gill: he lists other readings. One, "only let Him not set upon me," would show too much boldness, the kind of speech Job later repented of. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html

**v. 7** – Pulpit: at God's tribunal an upright man could appeal from God's justice to His mercy. With no Advocate yet revealed, Job's hope was reasonable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Clarke: the Hebrew word can mean "to victory" as well as "for ever." The Vulgate (the Latin Bible of the Catholic tradition) reads it that way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-23.html
– **Difference:** Wesley (Methodist) says this and similar sayings "cannot be excused from irreverence," and God later rebukes Job for them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html Gill reads "my Judge" as God, who clears Job for good, so that no human or devil can condemn him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html

**vv. 8–9** – Pulpit: the Hebrew words for forward, back, left and right also mean east, west, north and south, because people oriented themselves facing the sunrise. Job never doubts that God exists, only that he can perceive Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Wesley: God is absent "as a judge," though Job knew God is present everywhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html
– Guzik and Clarke: this is what a true seeker, or a genuine penitent, looks like. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/
– Gill: most Jewish commentators take these as compass directions. Cocceius read "forward/backward" as future and past time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html

**v. 10** – Guzik calls this a "bright flash of faith." God watches Job, is testing rather than punishing him, will end the trial and bring good from it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/
– Spurgeon: Job's confidence rests on God knowing him, and requires sincerity. Gold comes out of the fire proven and ready for use. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/23-10.html
– Pulpit: Job finally sees that affliction purifies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– **Difference over "gold":** Andersen (quoted by Guzik) says the image may mean the test simply proves Job was pure gold all along. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/ Clarke agrees: Job went into the furnace innocent and came out the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/23-10.html Barnes says trials actually purify piety. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/job/23-10.html
– Another reading, from the Cambridge Bible and Keil & Delitzsch on Bible Hub: "If He tried me, I should come forth as gold." Job means he would be cleared if God allowed a hearing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/23-10.htm
– Gill (Baptist): believers are precious only through grace and Christ's righteousness counted to them. He also gives Jewish readings where God avoids judging Job because He knows Job is innocent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html
– Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): Job sees the trial as God removing impurities. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/23-10.html

**v. 11** – Pulpit: "held close to His steps," meaning he kept as near God's path as possible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Wesley: the "steps" are the paths God appointed for people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html
– Matthew Henry: whatever hardships lie on God's path, we must keep pressing forward and never turn back. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_023.cfm

**v. 12** – Pulpit: "treasured up" is stronger than "esteemed." This verse points to an early revealed word from God before Scripture was written. Another possible reading is "more than my own law," meaning his own will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Spurgeon (via Guzik): Job had probably never seen Moses' books, yet God spoke to him. People then hid grain from raiders, and Job hid God's word even more carefully. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/
– Precept Austin: this verse is the secret of Job's endurance. Because he treasured and obeyed God's word, he knew God's character. https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_2312_commentary
– Gill: God's words are food for faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html

**v. 13** – Pulpit: complaint returns. God has not summoned Job and is unlikely to change (James 1:17). "Does what He desires" is a harsh way of saying God does what is best; Job doesn't think God acts on whim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Guzik: Job trusts God but knows he can't *make* God do anything. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-23/
– Matthew Henry (on Job 42) notes that Job said this "passionately, complaining." By ch. 42 he says it gladly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/42-5.html

**v. 14** – Pulpit: God will carry out what He has decreed for Job, and has other troubles He could still send. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Wesley: "many such things" means many examples of God dealing with people this way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html
– Matthew Henry: what is appointed can't be altered, which may silence us. Knowing that God appointed the affliction on the way to eternal glory can even satisfy us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_023.cfm
– Keil & Delitzsch: Job is reasoning from his present troubles to what lies ahead for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/23-17.htm

**v. 15** – Pulpit: Job fears further suffering and shrinks from God's unseen presence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Keil & Delitzsch: Job feels like a target of God's hostility, though he has done nothing to deserve it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/23-17.htm

**v. 16** – Pulpit: "faint" as in Lev. 26:36. The verb for "terrified" is very strong, meaning filled with horror. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm
– Gill: this isn't the soft, repentant heart grace gives, but a heart broken and melting under God's hand. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-23.html
– Wesley: his heart is bruised and melted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html

**v. 17** – **The translation matters most here.** The KJV reads: "Because I was not cut off before the darkness…"
– Pulpit and Wesley: Job grieves that he didn't die before calamity came, and that God didn't hide him (Wesley: in the grave). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/23.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/job-23.html
– Matthew Henry: the same idea. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_023.cfm
– Keil & Delitzsch reject the older reading. For them, what destroys Job is not the darkness itself but the sense that God is against him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/23-17.htm
– BSB, NIV and ESV ("not silenced") and Bible Hub's notes: Job refuses to be silenced. They see lament as an act of faith (Ps. 142). https://biblehub.com/job/23-17.htm
– Catholic: the Douay-Rheims reads "I have not perished because of the darkness." https://biblehub.com/niv/job/23-17.htm
– Gill gives a similar reading: Job marvels that he wasn't crushed to death by his afflictions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/23-17.htm
– Guzik: Job's strongest statements of faith come alongside equally strong fear. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/job-23/ (Spanish edition)
